catalog_quote: 2.3 Stress. Stress appears to be very irregular as it seems to occur on any syllable in a word. There is, however, an ordered system of rules governing stress placement in all words of two syllables or more. There are two levels of stress in addition to unstressed syllables. ... Stress is determined by three factors: vowel quality, syllable closure, and position in the word. A prefixal syllable, however, including a prefix resulting from reduplication, is almost never stressed, regardless of its other characteristics. The most important factor in stress assignment is vowel quality. A syllable with a nucleus of /a/ almost always receives primary stress regardless of position. 42) ... d. [ɸə.'tʰa.pʰʊs] 'quickly' ... j. [ˌqʰɔ.nəm.'sat] 'saddened'. When more than one syllable with a nucleus of /a/ occurs in a word, the last one is stressed as shown in (42i). (2) The classification rests on the primary SIL fieldwork phonology (1993) by the resident team, which is also the source behind StressTyp2, WALS and Dryer's 2013 reference grammar (Dryer has no original phonological data and restates the same rule, extracted text). sources.note: The only reachable scan (SIL REAP / Wayback, 30 pp) lacks printed p.110, which carries the secondary-stress rules and the exceptional/residue patterns that StressTyp2 paraphrases ('Secondary stress falls on the first syllable if primary stress occurs later than the second syllable...'; exceptional 'stress on the second syllable', ex. pʰeˈbogəˌnə); our srule field is currently filled from the OPD instead. Primary-stress coding is unaffected.

sources.quote: Instrumental pilot (1 speaker, Lauan dialect, 27 words/49 tokens) confirming contrastive H vs L tone (minimal pair /ŋót/ 'louse' vs /ŋòt/ 'to weed'). On stress: in Lithgow & Claassen's 1966 transcriptions 'H is always stress-bearing ... L is never stress-bearing'; authors' own auditory analysis found the most prominent syllable 'always involved H if it was present', but no F0/duration/intensity difference between stressed and unstressed L. sources.note: Only instrumental prosody study of Kara; establishes contrastive H/L tone realised only on accented syllables and explicitly leaves stress location undetermined -- grounds for a caution note that Kara word prosody involves lexical tone not mentioned by Schlie & Schlie 1993 (also flagged by Dryer 2013:4-5).
